title: Trump Signs Russia Sanctions Law, Clearing Path to 100% Tariffs on India
excerpt: The Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed Friday, authorizes tariffs of up to 100% on the top buyers of Russian energy — a list that includes India and China.
body:
• President Donald Trump signed H.R. 5334, the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” into law on Friday, September 18, 2026.
  • The law authorizes tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas — a list that includes India and China — and gives Trump wide discretion over rates, targets, and waivers.
  • It also sanctions Russian officials, banks, and the “shadow fleet” of tankers moving Russian energy, while extending existing Iran sanctions by five years.
  • The measure passed with large bipartisan margins, 86–11 in the Senate and 262–159 in the House, though critics warned it hands the president sweeping new tariff powers that could reach Europe as well.

President Donald Trump signed into law on Friday the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” which authorizes tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas — putting India and China, among Moscow’s biggest energy customers, directly in the crosshairs.

“On Friday, September 18, 2026, the President signed into law: H.R. 5334, the ‘Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,’ which authorizes and expands statutory sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran,” the White House said in a statement.

What the law does

The act directs the president to impose duties of up to 100% on goods imported from countries that rank among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or natural gas by total volume during the 12 months preceding enactment. A country is exempt from the gas-related duties if its Russian gas imports accounted for less than 15% of Russia’s total exports during the applicable period and it has taken “significant steps” to reduce those imports.

The law takes effect within 30 days of signing. It also sanctions Russian officials, banks, and the “shadow fleet” of tankers moving Russian energy, plus collaborators in Moscow’s defense industry — and extends U.S. sanctions on Iran by five years, an extension Trump insisted on before backing the bill.

Trump retains wide discretion over implementation — which countries face tariffs, the rates, and waivers. The measure is designed to starve President Vladimir Putin of resources for the war in Ukraine, now more than four years old.

A bipartisan legacy

The bill is a final legacy for the late Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican and close Trump ally who built bipartisan support for it before his unexpected death in July, shortly after returning from Ukraine. His sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to complete his Senate term.

“I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day. I know he would be so proud. Lindsey believed this bill, which he worked on for well over a year, would help end the war through squeezing Putin economically and forcing his customers to reevaluate their relationship with Russia.”

— Darline Graham, U.S. Senator

Co-drafted by Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut, with the House version introduced by Representative Michael McCaul of Texas, it cleared the Senate 86–11 and the House 262–159 on Wednesday evening after more than a year in the works. “Putin is a thug who understands only force and strength, which is what we must show clearly and unequivocally,” Blumenthal said. Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, welcomed the signing as a “powerful step” for Ukrainians.

The criticism

Despite the margins, the bill drew sharp Democratic criticism over fears Trump could use the expanded tariff authority for fresh levies on the European Union and elsewhere. “Why in the world would this Congress or the People’s House give this president unfettered authority to visit more tariffs on the world that will have an adverse economic impact on the American people?” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said during the debate. “I can’t do it.”

Securing Trump’s sign-off took fits and starts: the White House had to be convinced he would retain enough flexibility on sanctions first.

What it means for India

India sits squarely in the law’s line of fire. As one of the largest buyers of Russian crude, New Delhi is exposed to duties of up to 100% unless Trump grants a waiver or India qualifies under the reduction carve-outs — forcing it to weigh the economics of Russian energy against a punishing American tariff wall.

What to watch

With the law taking effect within 30 days, the question is how Trump uses his discretion: which countries he names, what rates he sets, where he grants waivers. India’s diplomatic response — and whether the threat pushes New Delhi to diversify energy purchases — will shape the next chapter, while Europe watches whether the powers stay aimed at Moscow’s customers.
image_caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin at a meeting in Moscow (left) and US President Donald Trump (right). Trump has signed the Russia sanctions bill into law, clearing the way for 100% tariffs on India and China over Russian oil purchases.
nri_angle: India is among the top purchasers of Russian crude targeted by the new law, so the 100% tariff authority directly threatens Indian exports and the U.S.-India trade relationship that diaspora businesses depend on.
author: Diaspora Desk
